subtopic: NORTHERN LOAN PROGRAM TO DEVELOP MINERAL RESOURCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: NORTHERN LOAN PROGRAM TO DEVELOP MINERAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wish to announce the government's decision to recommend to the house the adoption of a new northern loan program as an incentive to develop the mineral resources in the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
Exploration expenditures in the north have been running at an annual rate of approximately twenty millions of dollars per year which, while gratifying in terms of the past, is still unsatisfactory as compared with the oil and gas exploration expenditures in southern Canada in the magnitude of $150 million per annum.
The government therefore believes it is desirable to encourage greater northern exploration for the purpose of realizing the mineral possibilities which exist in these territories. The federal government has a net expenditure in the north every year of over $50 million. Companies and individuals engaged in the oil and mineral business presently appear to have adequate incentives under the Income Tax Act for exploration expenditure. The government proposes, 23033-1171
through a northern mineral development loan fund, to bring many of these same advantages to the ordinary Canadian investor and thereby considerably expand the funds available for such exploration.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The loan fund is for Canadians and Canadian-controlled companies only. While we welcome foreign capital in the north, we believe that Canadians should have a special incentive to invest in Canada's large northern potential of resources. Development in depth is one of our great challenges.
The loan fund will provide amounts of up to 40 per cent of approved exploratory expenditures to companies and individuals not eligible for the Income Tax Act charge-off incentive, and repayment will be required only if minerals are found in commercial quantities. The government will thereby assist with the high risks normally associated with northern resource exploration. The loan fund will be limited initially to $3 million per year, with possible increases in succeeding years after review of the program's success. An appropriate item will be included in estimates for the approval of the house.
In conclusion, I hope this loan fund will be instrumental in attracting major new exploration funds to the northern territories, and increasing the proportion of Canadian ownership in the non-renewable resources of the north.

subtopic: NORTHERN LOAN PROGRAM TO DEVELOP MINERAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to thank the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, for the second time in two sitting days, for paying the opposition the courtesy of sending his announcement on motions across to us ahead of time, because this gives us an opportunity to prepare some form of constructive response to such announcements.
The first point I wish to make is that the announcement today recognizes something that has been a fact for a long time, namely that United States tax laws and Canadian tax laws work in a similar direction to encourage United States investment in Canada and to penalize Canadian investment in the Canadian mining and oil industries. This fact was pointed out very clearly by the Gordon
February 28, 1966
1842	COMMONS
Northern Mineral Resources Program royal commission and the Borden royal commission, and the proposal announced today is a method to try and equalize the scales.
The proposal suggests a 40 per cent loan, not repayable if there is no success in the exploration. The only thing I would like to suggest here is that since the government intends to collect back the 40 per cent loan in a case where there is success in locating new oil or minerals, why not go one step further and take a 40 per cent interest in equity ownership? This would be the next logical step.
The proposal announced today carries on the over-all idea of dynamic action by the federal government in the development of the resources of this country that we brought into effect in a major way in 1957-58.
I should also like to point out, with respect to the expenditure of federal moneys in development of the north that we have to keep the economics in mind. That is, we cannot spread such a program generally all over the north. It has to be concentrated in those areas where there is the best chance relating to marketing the product. Therefore it is sound to go into the north from the sea, as I know the minister is interested in doing, via Baffin Island, and also through the land mass of the four western provinces.
I would also suggest that while this loan program which will encourage money to be spent in the high risk enterprise of exploration, giving companies a write-off where a write-off is not available to them now because they have not got refineries or smelters, the minister can help even more by restoring the roads to resources program. The hopes for a smelter at Great Slave lake will help, but by building a road connection around Great Slave lake in a circle the rich area around Great Slave lake could be made available for development through this loan fund program.
I should like to conclude with one little statement to the house. In 1958 and 1959 we invested $2J million in building three bridges in the Yukon over the Stewart, Pelly and Yukon rivers. Every two years since those three bridges were completed the federal government has received back $2J million in direct taxes as a result of that investment. This type of thing announced by the minister will have a similar result.

subtopic: NORTHERN LOAN PROGRAM TO DEVELOP MINERAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too desire to thank the minister for giving us notice of his intention to make this statement on motions. I am sure all hon. members will agree with the need for


development in the north and the need for additional exploration and development of minerals. I am sure they will also agree that this is a high risk area.
I think the minister is to be commended for setting up this northern mineral development fund. However, I am somewhat perturbed at the proposal that a borrower may be able to borrow up to 40 per cent of the amount invested and need not repay this loan unless he discovers minerals in commercial quantities. It seems to me this is coming fairly close to a "heads you win, tails I lose" proposition.
I think the minister could accomplish what he has in mind by entering into an arrangement with these companies whereby, an additional royalty in addition to the normal royalty, or 40 per cent of the profits made would be payable to the government by the company; and of course if the company made no profits they would not have to make any repayment. But if they do make profits in developing these resources, which after all belong to the people of Canada, I see no reason why the people of Canada should not have a share of the profits which result therefrom.
I hope the minister will give this some consideration. Also I hope that after the passage of time the amount of $3 million will be greatly expanded, because larger amounts of capital will be needed if we are to develop the northern parts of this country.

subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL PLANNING COMMITTEE
NATIONAL CAPITAL PLANNING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
1.	Has the National Capital Commission appointed a national capital planning committee as provided for in section 9	(3) of the National
Capital Act?
2.	If so, who are the members of the committee and what powers and functions have been assigned to it?
3.	If not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL PLANNING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
1, 2, 3. In 1946, the Federal District Commission established a national capital planning committee to draw up a master plan for the development, improvement, and beautification of the national capital district. The administrative staff serving the committee was provided by the Federal District Commission. The planning consultant was Mr. Jacques Greber, who was assisted by a Canadian staff called the national capital planning service.
The national capital committee held 22 meetings between October 30, 1946 and December 29, 1955. In 1954, the national capital planning service, which assisted Mr. Greber, and the national capital planning committee, was transferred to the Federal District Commission. Subsequently, the national capital planning committee met only four times; and the Federal District Commission, assisted by its staff and the advisory committees, carried out the work previously done by the national capital planning committee. Moreover, as the municipalities increased their own planning staffs, they required less assistance from the national capital planning committee.
The Federal District Commission Act was replaced by the National Capital Act, 1958, 7 Elizabeth II, Ch. 37. The National Capital Commission, whose responsibilities resemble those of the Federal District Commission, is assisted by the staff of the commission, the executive committee, the land committee, the advisory committee on design, the Gatineau Park advisory committee, the historical advisory committee, the information advisory committee, and by various consultants.
Given its modus operandi, the commission has not felt the need to make use of the authority conferred by the National Capital Act, s. 9(3), to appoint a national capital planning committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries):

subtopic: LOBSTER TRAP LIMIT, P.E.I.
speechtext:

However, there is now, and has been for some time, a regulation which stipulates that except with the permission of the minister no person shall, during the open season for any year in a district, or portion of a district, use for lobster fishing any boat that has been used during that year for lobster fishing in any other district. speechtext:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: 'REQUEST FOR ESCALATOR CLAUSE IN SUPERANNUATION ACT
speechtext:

The answer to part 2 is as follows:
In my reply to this point raised by the secretary treasurer of the Federal Superannuates' National Association, I referred to the problem of financing increases in the pensions of federal superannuates, which would involve a charge on either general revenues or the superannuation account. I said that the government does not feel justified in granting, at the expense of the public generally, a special treatment which was not received by other retired Canadians, and that because the full amount of the credit of the superannuation account was needed to meet charges on the account on the existing basis, payment of increased pensions from the account would not be actuarily sound.

February 28, 1966	COMMONS
Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and follows up remarks attributed to him over the week end relating to the conservation of water resources in Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question very often comes up; when are we going to have a national water policy? It is quite difficult for me to answer this question, because everybody knows the provinces have a lot to do with natural resources; with water in particular.
I do not think hon. members should be pessimistic. A lot of good work is being done in this field at the moment. For example, a study has been started of the Ontario northern rivers. Another study is proceeding on water levels in the great lakes. About ten days ago the Minister of Agriculture and I were in Winnipeg discussing with representatives of the three prairie provinces the setting up of a board for the investigation of the Nelson and Saskatchewan basins. The conversation is going along very nicely and we are about to reach agreement in principle.
I would remind hon. members that although we do not have a sort of unitary water policy, we are nevertheless making great progress in federal-provincial relations in this field.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall vote No. 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, naturally we are awaiting with bated interest the reply that will be given by the Minister of Justice to the various questions that have been propounded and are as yet unanswered. I intend to deal now with only two matters while awaiting the response of the minister regarding questions that are of pre-eminent importance.
During the question period I asked the Prime Minister whether his attention had been drawn to the views expressed over the week end by the minister of justice of the province of Quebec and what the government's stand would be respecting the convening of a royal commission to look fully into the whole field of crime. Canadians as a whole have been shocked, even dumbfounded by the revelations of the last year or so, and
Supply-Justice
everywhere there is a demand that the situation be looked into to see whether the administration of justice has been subject to infiltration by gangs, thugs and Mafia dominated individuals. I think the demand for a royal commission which I had the honour to make months ago has been reinforced by events during the passing months.
Only on Friday the hon. member for Yukon again repeated that request. I cannot understand the government's position. The government has before it the facts revealed in the Dorion Commission inquiry and the complaints that have been made by the Ontario Crime Commission respecting the failure of the Department of Justice to reply to letters regarding international criminals. These things make one wonder why a royal commission representative not only of the federal government but the provinces should not be set up.
The division of responsibility in the administration of justice demands that there be representation from both jurisdictions on the commission. The Prime Minister stated today that this matter was before a dominion-provincial conference. That is no answer. More and more fields of endeavour that should be before the House of Commons are receiving the attention of dominion-provincial conferences and the House of Commons representing the people receives little or no information regarding these matters.
I would simply quote the words of the minister of justice of the province of Quebec who stated over the week end:
Organized crime has created a "veritable state of emergency". . . . "It has become more and more evident that organized crime, not only in Quebec but in the whole of the country, has created a veritable state of emergency." . . .
Mr. Wagner recalled that a royal commission investigation into crime is not a new idea-he had made the same suggestion when he was Crown Attorney and when he was a Judge of the court of sessions here.
"What I had in mind then is precisely a commission of national scope which would bring witnesses from all corners of the country because it is now public knowledge that organized crime knows no provincial boundaries. A local inquiry would not uncover what a royal commission or what a national commission would reveal."
The support of the minister of justice of the province of Quebec, a man who has had experience both as a prosecutor and as a local judge, gives added emphasis to the need of action in this regard.
I am now going to refer to the Spencer case because I want the minister to know and the Prime Minister too that it is not a dead

February 28, 1966
Supply-Justice
issue. We want the facts. More and more it is becoming a question of whether or not the government can stand against public opinion which generally has demanded an investigation into the circumstances, the strange, bizarre circumstances of the Spencer case. It is parliament's responsibility. It has been interesting to find that while up to very recently, outside of the press across Canada which is almost unanimous in a demand for action in this regard, we in the opposition had not been able to secure support from members sitting on the Liberal benches supporting the government, the other day there were revelations. One was by the hon. member for York-Humber in a most striking presentation. There was no evasion, there was a directness in the expression of his view which cannot be wiped aside.
Even in the mind of the hon. member for Verdun, who has a reputation for qualified viewpoints, suspicion is beginning to be aroused. He wants to know why no action has been taken. "What action there has been, has been bureaucratic, dictatorial, and completely without precedent. This man was designated by the Minister of Justice. He found his way on to the television screens of this country and he designated this man and identified him. Earlier there had been some reference to him.
According to Lord Hewitt, "the only things that interfere with the absolute power of bureaucratic government are the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law". If a poll were taken of members of the house, I think it would be overwhelmingly in favour of the need for investigation into this weird case. Let me point out how difficult it is to obtain information. The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose on January 21 placed the following questions on the order paper and they have hibernated there ever since:
1.	Were alleged security or espionage offences committed by Victor G. Spencer, now of Vancouver and, if so, what were they and when did these alleged offences take place?
2.	What year did he come to Canada, and from what country?
Who is hiding the facts here? Sir, is it not strange that questions like these remain on the order paper for a month and ten days without being answered. What are they hiding? What are they concealing? What are they afraid of? I realize that this government has established an international reputation as a bumbler. Indeed, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, speaking on

international affairs the other day in Edmonton, said, "we have to stumble to a stalemate". That is what this government has done. That is its policy, its attitude; it refuses to face facts.
All across this nation there is a demand for action and the Prime Minister has intensified that demand by an explanation which certainly did not explain. Indeed, the Montreal Star, which never has been known as one of the government's most active critics, on February 25 said in an editorial headed "The Spencer Case Is Not Closed":
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
So far as Mr. Pearson is concerned the Spencer case is closed. The Prime Minister may be happy about it all, quite convinced that the interests of national security are not jeopardized, and that no injustice has been worked. No one else is so easily convinced and the suspicion will not down that in this, as in perhaps other cases, the government has something to hide. It has at any rate fumbled and can satisfy the public that justice has been done only by bringing Spencer to trial or instituting a judicial inquiry.
I immediately add that when the government says security procedures might be revealed I accept that explanation, but that does not justify the refusal to call together an inquiry presided over by a judge or judges sitting in camera. We want to know whether the rights of Canadians can be shamelessly swept aside.
The last paragraph of this article states:
Objections to the government's course of action in the Spencer case are not based on sympathy for Spencer. He himself created the publicity that now surrounds him by identifying himself in connection with the ousting of two Russian representatives. What gives cause for concern is the government's assumption that whenever it sees fit it can sidestep justice and deal with people as if we were living in a police state.
That is what has happened here. Surely the shades of 1945 and 1946 are not returning. I intend to ask questions to which we want answers. These are not questions that will interfere with national security but we want to know about a few of the things that have been hidden in fog, smokescreen and mystery to such an extent that people are beginning to wonder why the government has hidden them if there is nothing to hide.
Let us consider how the government started in this matter. It began by giving the explanation that Mr. Spencer had to be subjected to what one would call protective surveillance in order to protect the nation. Then the minister let the cat out of the bag when he said: We are not doing it for that reason because he never endangered the
February 28, 1968

security of the state. The security of the state is not in jeopardy because he is wandering around wherever he may be.
The second explanation was that they were protecting him.

There was mention of previous cases. What was done in previous cases where complete secrecy was maintained? No names were given in those cases. Why is this man denied a hearing? What stage have we reached in this country when a Canadian, whatever his record may be, and apparently it cannot be very serious because the minister says that the security of the nation was never in danger, is told that he is out of a job but wherever he goes he is going to have somebody with him? If that is not a form of open arrest I do not know what else it is.
The government decided that the first explanation was not very good because it gave all the earmarks of a police state, and they altered it. What a tangled web of circumstances. The explanation was then given that he was being followed in order to provide protection of his own person, because they do not want him to be subjected to physical danger from the communists, but surely nobody believes that possible.
Surely no one could be gullible enough to accept the first theory that he was being followed to assure that he would do no wrong and then the amended form, that he is being followed for that purpose and also to preserve his precious being. Let us get the story straight. These people cannot have it both ways. In a democratic state there is certainly a difference between protection by law enforcement officers and surveillance of a person because he might commit a criminal offence. If it was intended for the sake of protection, all I say is that even a lawyer without experience would not have used the word "surveillance". I suggest these people changed their story to meet the criticism. There can be no justification for this nation putting anyone under protective custody or keeping him under open arrest in the circumstances that have been revealed so far.
I was not in the house at the time but I was amazed to know that the Prime Minister had said, as reported at page 1683 of Hansard for February 23:
I do not believe his rights as a person or as a citizen have been violated.
Supply-Justice
I should like to ask at what stage he would consider rights to have been violated if this is not a violation. He said that Spencer had not complained. Have they interviewed him or have the R.C.M.P. interviewed him to find out whether he basks in the sunshine of notoriety with police officers on his trail wherever he goes? Has there been any correspondence with him? Surely it would not interfere with security of the state if this were revealed.
The explanation that has been given, the secondary revised version, is nothing but pharasaic cant and hypocrisy. The government started out by saying that this man was being followed and kept under surveillance. Surveillance means the following of a person for the purpose of assuring that he does not commit a crime or to ascertain whether or not evidence can be obtained against him regarding a crime.
Surely there can be no successful denial of this fair request for a judicial inquiry behind closed doors. Such an inquiry would permit a judicial declaration whether security would be harmed if this man were given his day in court. I hope never again will a royal commission be subjected to a suggestion by the Prime Minister or any other minister of the government to the effect that its findings do not meet the sensibilities of the Prime Minister or another minister and that the evidence given under oath should be changed and altered by an ex-parte statement not under oath. Surely that case of asking a judge to change his judgment after it had been delivered and tabled in parliament was the height of indiscretion and worse.
The Prime Minister laughs. He got in touch with the head of a royal commission and said: Your finding is not right.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The former minister of justice said, "That is what I said, but what I should have said when I did not say it was what I would have said if I had thought it over. This is what it will be." What nonsense is this? It was one of the most serious invasions of judicial independence that has ever been seen in this country. Yet they smile. One remembers the words of William Cullen Bryant which are as true today as when they were uttered, "O freedom, close not your eyes. Its opposition never sleeps." What we are asked to do in this case is say, "Begone, freedom. Exit the rights of individuals who only ask that they be tried for their alleged wrongs."

February 28, 1966
Supply-Justice
Why is no action being taken in the Spencer case? It is for the government to say. They have had to change their story as to the reason he is being followed. Why? Spencer said, "If they do anything with me, heads will swim". Whose heads? What heads? A little later, on December 26, Mr. Peter Trueman reported in his column that Spencer had said that if the federal government prosecuted him on espionage charges, high-ranking officials in Ottawa would suffer. Those are strong words. Who are these heads? The former minister of justice, with that urbanity he shows whenever justice is trampled on, smiles and sneers. I say to him: Who are these people?
There should be a royal commission, behind closed doors if necessary. I will go along with the government on that even though I do not like closed-door investigations. But under the circumstances an inquiry should be conducted by a judge if there is danger of the revelation of counter-espionage. A judge can hear, sift and conclude. Surely we have not come to the stage in this country where a person can be named, charged with a heinous crime, the most serious crime against the state, publicly branded and maintained in a state of continuing open arrest without a proper inquiry.
The excuse might be offered: Well, this man tried to undermine the state; therefore he should not have the rights of all other citizens. If that press release was based on fact, everything about his conduct was despicable and worthy of punishment. But to condone wrongdoing on the part of the state on the ground that the wrongdoing by the victim might reveal certain information is anything but what one should expect. Even at this late date there should be an inquiry into this matter. When I raised this question the Prime Minister at first said he would consider it even though the Minister of Justice had swept it aside. What a sinuous course the present Minister of Justice followed. When the election was on he said, "I am not looking into the case."
I will be very glad to quote the speech of the Minister of Justice in this regard because I always come with the necessary material. He said he was not looking into the case then. That is what he said and I shall quote from the speech in a moment. Then he left the impression that there would be an investigation along the line of a commission. Once the

election was over and that sort of attitude had achieved its purpose, suddenly he changed his viewpoint.
I point out that across the country, as I said a moment ago, the press almost unanimously demands action. La Presse, the Globe and Mail, Le Devoir, the Montreal Star, the Gazette, the Toronto Telegram-everywhere, without regard to party considerations, there is a demand for action. But this government stands adamant. Why? Whose heads will roll? What revelations will be made? Sir, that is what parliament is for, to see that the nation's security shall be protected and the rights of the individual shall not be denied unnecessarily.
Even in the days of war, as the hon. member for York South said, a man had greater rights. During the days of World War II I sat on the committee considering the defence of Canada regulations. Many persons were interned because of the exigencies of war who later had to be released. In this case, sir, the Bill of Rights has been shockingly violated. There has been a gross perversion of the elementary principles of right. I say, on the basis of very full study, that what has been done to Spencer serves neither justice nor national security. He has been scourged by despotism. He has been denied human rights. The government that will not place him in the dock will place him forever in a pillory.
Surely ordinary justice demands that a man be judged according to law. This man has been judged outside the law. He has been convicted without evidence by the jury of public opinion. He has been punished without verdict. For the rest of his life he carries with him the stigma of a traitor to his country.
I have some questions I want answered, although on the basis of information to date it is with trepidation that I even advance them. I am going to read, because I think it should be on the record, the press release issued by the Department of External Affairs on May 8. Before I do, I ask the minister to reveal this fact; it cannot interfere with the security of the nation. Was it in the month of January or February or March or April that the first suspicions came to the attention of the Department of Justice regarding the proclivities of this man or did the wrongdoing only come to light a day or so prior to May 8? [DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This is very important. When this matter was revealed that great body of men, the R.C.M.P., was under attack in connection
February 28, 1966

with the Dorion inquiry. How did it come about that the Spencer case, at that significant moment, should be brought to light? If the alleged offences took place in the month of April or early May it is understandable. When did these alleged offences take place?
They say they have no evidence. On more than one occasion wrongdoers, communists, who have come into Canada to undermine the state have been told to get out; they have been sent back. Indeed, the experience of our country, the United States and the United Kingdom has been that many of these people who come in under the guise of diplomacy use that as a camouflage for wrongdoing against the country to which they are accredited. Let us read what this press release says:
The Department of External Affairs today announced that the ambassador of the Soviet Union was requested on May 4 to arrange for the departure from Canada of two members of his mission, Mr. A. E. Bytchkov, of the Commercial Section, and a Chancery clerk, Mr. V. N. Polu-chkin.
I pause here to suggest that a man in the commercial section, who did not enjoy diplomatic immunity, was allowed to leave. I am talking about the commercial section.
The Canadian government had learned that they had engaged in activities incompatible with their official status and had, therefore, found it necessary to declare them persona non grata. They left Canada on May 7.
Listen to this, and this is the Department of External Affairs speaking:
In one instance a Canadian civil servant was paid thousands of dollars to gather information and documentation in Canada, the purpose of which was to assist in the establishment of espionage activities in Canada and other countries, and to perform economic intelligence tasks, including the provision of detailed information on the Transmountain pipe line system in western Canada.
The question I ask is this: Many thousands of dollars were paid to this man Spencer according to this record but today you say you have no evidence sufficient to convict. You issue this statement on the eighth day of May. In what other countries were these espionage establishments to be brought about? This information would not reveal anything of importance to our security. You have already said thousands of dollars were paid. We ask, how many? Let us see how big this is. How many individuals were approached by this man. How much was paid to him? You must have all this information. How many payments were made and over what period of time? Let us have that information. The security of this nation will not be undermined by this information.
Supply-Justice
Then, what about the naturalized Canadian citizen who was paid thousands of dollars to provide technical information? He is free because he assisted. Of what is he free? His name remains among the great incognitos of our country. What did he do? He endeavoured to compromise other Canadians, including female employees of the government, with the object of securing their assistance in obtaining access to classified information. The minister shakes his head in a horizontal motion, which means no. This is what it says in the press release from which I am reading issued by the Department of External Affairs. The Minister of Justice says there is nothing in that. What kind of press release is this to emanate from the Department of External Affairs containing information that is false?
The press release says this man was given specialized photographic training to assist him in his task. Is that true? This is true. Well, we are getting along. The minister says it is not true, he shook his head in a negative way, that this man tried to compromise female employees in an effort to obtain access to information. You see, the minister is very honest and straightforward about this. He says that is not a fact. What kind of reliance can you place on a press release issued by the minister of the Department of External Affairs-it would not be issued by him but by somebody there-when the Minister of Justice says it has no foundation? We are starting to get some information.
I quote again from the press release:
The approaches made by the two members of the Soviet Embassy very shortly came to the attention of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As a result of this co-operation by conscientious Canadians, the police were able to establish the improper intent of the Soviet approaches and to put an end to them before any damage was done to Canadian interests.
I ask, when was this? When did these things happen? I am amazed to have an admission from the Minister of Justice that the cornerstone upon which the government has founded this press release by the Department of External Affairs has cracks in it; parts of it are not time. This is a very serious matter. I know the minister will want to clear this matter up beyond peradventure. It is in that spirit that I appeal to him once more that action be taken in the interests of justice. The very fact he now admits part of the press release was without foundation indicates the need for a royal commission to go into this matter.

February 28. 1966
Supply-J ustice
Let me go on from there. One man gets thousands of dollars. He obtained the money to begin with because they had to trust him first and then later, because of conscience, fear or whatever the reason, a change was brought about in his thinking. Do you not think a commission should have an opportunity of looking into this situation, because thousands of dollars are not paid by the Soviets just for the amusement of making payments? I have just been reading the papers of the Russian spy-his name has gone out of my mind for the moment but he was the Russian colonel who was executed-and they indicate that the results are not insignificant.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Surely, Mr. Chairman, in view of that admission by the Minister of Justice, which I am sure came as a surprise to the Prime Minister and the other ministers, there is no difficulty now in making a case for a commission. I do not in any way wish to see our security techniques revealed. On the other hand, the present state of indefiniteness, uncertainty and evasion in this matter, the foundation story now ceasing to exist with the admission by the minister that one portion of this press release is not factual, point to the need for action to be taken.
I am not going to press this case further at this time. However, the Minister of Justice mentioned a moment ago that one statement I had made was not quite correct. I have before me the file. So far as the R.C.M.P. is concerned, the commissioner received severe criticism in the Dorion report. The attitude taken toward two of the high officials of the R.C.M.P. by the judge before he published his report indicated that there would be criticism. When the Spencer case was first revealed the Dorion report was being written.
The minister indicated a moment ago-I want to be entirely fair about this report-that he went right after this as soon as he became Minister of Justice. I think fairness demands that I admit that. I admit-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman explain what he means when he says that I went right after this? Right after what?
Mr. Chairman, I would think that with that assiduity and energy that the hon. gentleman possesses in such abundant measure, as soon as the matter came into his hands-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What matter?

-he would have acted. And he did act. I was just going to pay a tribute to him for his action but I do not want to spoil the record. I have before me an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of July 8 written by Mr. Geoffrey Stevens in which the following appears:
The short, easy-going lawyer from Sorel, Que., moved smoothly and swiftly yesterday into the political hot-seat . . . Without waiting for the official swearing-in ceremony, he set up a meeting-
Then the article goes on to say this, and it is a very striking statement for a minister who is just assuming the heavy responsibilities of Minister of Justice:
-although he could not sympathize with the violent attacks made on the R.C.M.P. last week by the French-speaking members of the Social Credit Party and the Social Credit Rally, he felt there must be some basis for the M.P.'s complaints.
"I feel there is nothing fundamentally wrong (with the R.C.M.P.) but I hope to get at the reason very quickly"-
That is why I mentioned, Mr. Chairman, he had moved forward with acceleration and dispatch. Then the article went on to say that the minister also had other hot potatoes to dispose of such as Adrien Meunier, Leo Landreville and so on. The hon. member for Hochelega also became involved in this and wrote an article in the Toronto Telegram dated August 24 in which he covered a lot of things. In his article he said:
In his report published at the beginning of July, he criticized our federal police corps-
He is referring to Chief Justice Dorion.
-so severely that many Canadians, including this columnist, are still wondering why nothing happened to Commissioner McLellan as a consequence of such a dressing down.
I did not hold that view, but this article was written by a very eminent publicist. However, he gets to the bottom of things because he went on to say:
Not only did Chief Justice Dorion condemn the R.C.M.P. for its appalling lack of bilingualism, an aspect of the problem that could be deemed by many as not directly relevant to the case, but he also described the handling of the Rivard affair as a very poor performance by the force.
It is now official, thanks to the report, that the R.C.M.P. went to work after a long delay that it could not explain; that the methods displayed by its men were unworthy of a responsible institution.
Then he goes on to say:
The press was unanimous in demanding that Guy Favreau resign but to my knowledge, only one newspaper suggested that Commissioner McLellan was in the same situation.
February 28, 1966

That article indicates the opinion of a most outstanding publicist, now one of those who, having seen the light of day, sits on the thrones of the powerful.
Then we go on to follow the course through. I say advisedly that I am concerned about the Royal Canadian Mounted Police being placed in any invidious position which would result in the loss to any degree of the kind of prestige they have built up. I speak as one who, before I became a member of parliament, was in the courts and I met with them week after week in literally hundreds of cases. I relied upon them, and in all the times I appeared before the courts there were only two cases in which there was ever any evidence given by a mounted policeman which I had any reason to believe was not the truth and the whole truth.
However, in this case, strangely enough, they do have to start to produce an answer, which is a serious situation. That is why on Friday I mentioned the fact that the commissioner of the mounted police must keep out of participating in any way in the defence of his force, however strongly he may feel about the matter. That is a question for the minister. As soon as a person occupying the position of commissioner starts getting into that field, controversy takes place. Not everybody will accept the views expressed by him and the result is one not beneficial to the maintenance of that high degree of regard which the R.C.M.P. enjoys.
I am concerned about what has happened over the last couple of years. I will say no more at this time, but I do hope that never again will the commissioner get into a field of controversy. Let him talk about the work of the mounted police, give the benefit of his ideas and experiments and so on, but he must never be in the category of a protagonist for one side or another. The history of police forces stands out as a warning that to take such a course may lead to serious consequences.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I said the minister started right in. Then I said he decided to put off consideration of the case until after the election, on November 3, according to an article by David Scott, the Minister of Justice said that when he got the chance to study the report, the report on Spencer I take it, he would decide whether there was sufficient evidence. Then somebody said to him: "What about his statement 'Heads will swim'?" To this the minister replied that the man should tell his story to the
Supply-Justice
police, whatever it was. He added: "The implications in the man's statement suggest he may have a political axe to grind."
I ask this question: Did the mounted police interview Spencer as to what he meant by this outrageous threat? Then the minister said, according to this report: "I don't know what it is he has to say but whatever it is, let him go ahead and say it. I would be very interested to see it myself." This commendable interest of the minister is widely shared by those of us who want to get the facts.
Then the minister gave an interview on November 5 to the Toronto Star in which he said he found the whole affair "pretty strange". I think there is agreement with that. The article states:
In a telephone interview Mr. Cardin added that he understands the man told the newspaper that if he were able to do so he "would tell everything and that heads would swim."
The Minister of Justice said he will deal further with the case on his return to Ottawa after the election.
Then I demanded a probe. I wanted information. We have not been able to get that information. But we were told the reason Spencer was not being prosecuted was that he was sick. I have a quotation to this effect if it is wanted. Hon. gentlemen opposite said, "If only this man was well". I recall the old saying: "When the devil was sick, the devil a monk would be".
Now this man is well. The first excuse was: We cannot prosecute because he is under surgery. You know, the story as one unravels it makes me wonder. It is a difficult thing to follow. Finally there was the decision that in no circumstances would action be taken. I lay these quotations aside for use a little later. I simply rest my case here at this time. Try to unravel this tortuous course. There was the press statement which got headlines all over the world. Here was the R.C.M.P. finding this wrongdoer who would be undermining other countries by the setting up of espionage rings elsewhere. Out went the Russians. One of them did not have diplomatic protection but he was allowed to go home. Then the man was too sick for proceedings against him to be taken. Follow it through. I know the minister will straighten out this labyrinth when he speaks. We would be delighted to have an acceptable explanation though I doubt that his power of advocacy will be sufficient to assure this.
Sweeping everything aside, I now ask the government to have the fullest investigation. The people of Canada have the right to know

February 28, 1968

what is what. The R.C.M.P. have the right to know. This man has the right to know. If this be not so, then any time when one would remove a person against whom there was not sufficient evidence one would do it simply by stating a fact, as was stated repeatedly in this press release, and when the press release, untrue and unjustified in part as the minister admits, had served its purpose no further action would be taken. I rest.

Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question? I believe I heard him correctly. He said that on two occasions he found that the R.C.M.P. were not up to par. I notice that speaking in the debate on October 25, 1963 on security matters he said, as found on page 4049 of Hansard.
In the hundreds of cases in which I participated, only in one did I find on the part of any member of that force a departure from the elemental justice which has been characteristic of the force.

The hon. gentleman
would not be able to see any difference between those two statements. One dealt with one matter. The matter I had to discuss today deals entirely with credibility. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, members of this committee realize, I am sure, that security cases are for obvious reasons among the most difficult and delicate administrative problems of government, problems about which, unfortunately, very little can be said.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Those who have had responsibility for the administration of government or who have been in charge of the Department of Justice will perhaps feel and understand more keenly the difficulties involved in security cases. Indeed, while the Leader of the Opposition was prime minister security cases arose but questions let alone debates, about such cases were not accepted or answered on the ground that it would not be in the national interest to do so. We, then in opposition, accepted this attitude because, first, we knew and appreciated the inherent difficulties involved both nationally and internationally in dealing with security cases; second, because we realized the necessity of keeping secret the security procedures used by the police in these cases; third, because we had confidence

in the competence, loyalty and integrity of the R.C.M.P. and in the effectiveness of their counter-espionage activities; fourth, because we trusted the accuracy and the wisdom of the legal officers of the Department of Justice and believed in the sense of responsibility of the government and the common sense of the minister of justice, whoever he might be.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that without this basic confidence and trust, not only in the competence and loyalty of the civil service but also in the good faith and sense of responsibility of government and individual ministers, parliament will not and cannot work.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In recent times it has become dangerously easy to accuse and condemn by innuendos and insinuations without being called upon to substantiate charges. It may be considered politically expedient and even smart tactics, to create doubt and confusion in the house and among the public by asking questions and seeking information and explanations about this case, which is a bona fide security case, but I submit it is demagoguery for anyone to ask these questions knowing that the answers cannot and should not be given in public.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the field of national security and national security cases nothing has really changed since 1963. Security problems are as complex now as they were before 1963. Secrecy for security procedures is as essential now as it was then. The law officers of the Department of Justice are as knowledgeable and conscientious as they were in
1963.	The integrity and competence of the R.C.M.P. have not diminished.
Then what is it in the Spencer case that has motivated the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and other members of the committee to demand a judicial inquiry into this case and into the whole field of security procedures?
The whole action of the Minister of Justice.
The minister's conduct.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Was the right hon. gentleman not satisfied with the security procedures when he was head of the government? If not, why did he not have a royal commission
February 28, 1966

then? If he was satisfied then, why does he call for one now since the very same security procedures have been used in this case?
Is the right hon. gentleman complaining because I did not prosecute Spencer? If he is, is the right hon. gentleman saying that prosecutions were proceeded with in all security cases that came to his attention between 1957 and 1963? I am sure the right hon. gentleman is not saying that, and with reason.
How many were there?
Quite a few.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the right hon. gentleman questioning the validity and soundness of the recommendations of the law officers of the Crown that there was not sufficient admissible evidence to bring down a conviction against Spencer? If he is, then how can he reconcile this attitude with the severe criticism he addressed to my predecessor for not having sought the opinion of the legal officers of the Crown in the Denis case when these are the very same competent people? Is the right hon. gentleman suggesting that even though there was not a reasonable chance of bringing down a conviction I should have laid charges and prosecuted Spencer just the same and risk having disclosed the same security procedures about which his government question in the house on the grounds that it would not answer even the most benign was not in the public interest to do so?
With the experience that the right hon. gentleman has had in security matters when he was in office he must know or he can guess why prosecution did not take place in the Spencer case. If that is so, why is the right hon. gentleman acting as though he had never heard of security and intelligence procedures and why is he insinuating that the government has something to hide?
Is the right hon. gentleman condemning me because I advocated appropriate surveillance of a person who, of his own volition and without being forced to do so, admitted he was the man the R.C.M.P. were questioning in connection with espionage activities?
How could he deny it? Everybody knew it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the right hon. gentleman questioning the legality or propriety of the accepted procedure of surveillance? The right hon. gentleman has in fact severely criticized the government for not having maintained stricter surveillance over Hal Banks. Was the right hon. gentleman advocating an illegal procedure at that time?
Supply-Justice
Is the right hon. gentleman suggesting that surveillance can or should be applied only when a person has been charged or convicted? How then could the police carry out their responsibility in the field of prevention of crime?
The hon. member for Kamloops, for whom I have great esteem, is well acquainted with the difficulties involved in the handling of security cases and I am sure he will agree with me when I say that no minister of justice would have authorized a prosecution when his legal advisers had recommended that the evidence admissible in court could not and would not carry a conviction. I also feel quite sure that any minister of justice would be extremely sensitive to the possibility of divulging our counter-espionage activities.
If, Mr. Chairman, the security procedures applied by the R.C.M.P. in this case are the normal procedures always used, which have proven to be very effective in the past, if the rules and policy for the laying of charges and instituting of action are the same in this case as have been applied over the years, if surveillance by the police is a normal procedure for the prevention of crime, there can be and there is only one fact that is unprecedented in the Spencer case, something which the Leader of the Opposition and members of other political parties are scrupulously trying to ignore, forget, pass over and avoid mentioning, and that one unprecedented fact is that Spencer, not I, branded himself as a spy when he admitted he was the postal clerk involved in the espionage case.
You disclosed his name before the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He had done that before me and, Mr. Chairman, because he did identify himself, after the government took all necessary precautions to safeguard his identity, am I being asked to prosecute him even though I know that I could not convict him and that I would risk compromising our security procedures? If Spencer had not identified himself as the man involved in espionage activity, would hon. members of the committee have insisted on a trial? No, Mr. Chairman, they would not have insisted any more in this case than they did in other security cases in the past.

What date was it that the minister revealed Spencer's name?

February 28, 1966
Supply-Justice

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We will go into that later, Mr. Chairman. I did not interrupt the right hon. gentleman and if he will allow me to finish my speech, I will deal with his question afterwards.
What is the difference between this security case and other cases if it is not the unprecedented fact that the person involved in this case actually identified himself and branded himself as a spy of his own free will? And because Spencer decided to identify himself, should I be asked to ignore the well established policy in prosecutions and prosecute him anyway?

Oh, oh.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Big joke.
There were quite a number prosecuted in 1945-46.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Are you saying that you prosecuted all the security cases which came before you when you were in office?
They were never identified by a Minister of Justice.
They were not identified.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. May we let the Minister of Justice continue without interruption?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the government is being asked to have a judicial inquiry into the Spencer case. I can assure the members of the committee that I believe in the principle behind the setting up of royal commissions of inquiry of any kind when they are warranted, but I do not believe royal commissions and judicial inquiries should replace the basic trust and confidence which are essential in any form of responsible government. Nor, Mr. Chairman, do I believe that royal commissions should be substituted for the normal administration of government and for the due processes of law.
There is no due process here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not believe either that a royal commission or inquiry should be set up every time the opposition asks for one in order to prove that the government did the right thing.
What about the press of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is exactly what we would be doing in this case.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister allow a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be delighted to answer the question after I finish my speech.
After you finish reading it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I believe it would do a lot of good if the hon. member would write his own speeches. There would be a lot more logic in them than there is in the ones he has made here.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are reading Favreau's writing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question I should like to ask hon. members is, what exactly would the commission inquire into? Into the security procedures of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police? Why? The Royal Mounted Police actually were successful in detecting this security case among others and did eliminate any potential danger to the security of Canada and, even though it may not be generally known in Canada, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police's record in the field of counter-espionage is second to that in no other country in the world and their procedure and discipline in security matters is recognized internationally as one of the best in the world. Is there justification here for a royal commission into the security procedures of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?
No one suggested that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would the royal commission inquire into my decision not to prosecute Spencer? The basis of my decision is a long and well established practice applied by successive ministers of justice and, indeed, no other logical criteria could in fact be applied. Would this mean that a royal commission would be warranted to look into all future cases where prosecutions did not follow the investigation of security cases? Would the royal commission look into past cases under this or the previous government where prosecutions did not follow in similar investigations. If not, then why not? What difference is there? Where do you draw the line?
I might also ask whether we need a royal commission to tell us that surveillance is a normal and necessary procedure employed by police forces all over the world in carrying out their responsibility of maintaining order and preventing crime?
February 28, 1986
Protecting a man from danger.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We will go into that, if you give me time. Do we need to have a royal commission to confirm that Spencer identified himself and branded himself as the spy that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were questioning when all the newspapers in Canada carried the story of Spencer's selfidentification more than three weeks before I mentioned him on a television program?
No, no. What is the date? That is what I asked a while ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You will get the dates. Ask the hon. member for Bow River. He made my case the other day when he spoke.
You are not making it, so you need help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the hon. member for York South charge that Spencer is being discriminated against and unjustly treated because he was dismissed without pension and without appeal. Surely hon. members know that employment in the public service is during pleasure. This principle is applicable to all employees of the civil service including Spencer.
What happened to the collective bargaining rights?
You cannot fire anyone any time for any reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For reason and for cause.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, order. May I ask hon. members to permit the Minister of Justice to make his speech? If some hon. members wish to interject certain opinions they certainly will have an opportunity to do so when their turn comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the Public Service Superannuation Act pensions are paid to employees of the civil service as a right but under certain conditions. According to the Act an employee will be deprived of his pension if he is dismissed because of misconduct. This is applicable to all employees of the civil service and has been applied to other Canadian citizens in the public service. Why should it not apply to Spencer? Section 50 of the Civil Service Act, which was enacted in 1961 when the previous government was in office and after the Bill of Rights came into effect, does not provide for an appeal of the dismissal of an employee in certain cases. This law passed by the house was applied in the Spencer case.
Sup p ly-J ustice
I feel, Mr. Chairman, sure that hon. members will appreciate that in certain justified circumstances the government as an employer must take the hard decision to proceed under section 50 of the Civil Service Act and must take the responsibility for that decision. After a very painstaking examination of the whole situation, the government is satisfied as an employer that no injustice has been done and, Mr. Chairman, in clear conscience the government can assert that position.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
No one member or group of members in this house has a monopoly on genuine concern for the civil rights and liberties of individuals. We are all dedicated to and have all sworn to defend and protect these rights.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are also all dedicated to and have all sworn to safeguard our national security. The undeniable responsibility of the opposition to criticize constructively does not and cannot for obvious reasons always reflect the irreconcilable conflict which arises at times between these two fundamental principles to which we are all dedicated.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, the government in its undeniable responsibility to administer the country must take a decision, no matter how difficult that decision is or may be. As I have said, the government has done this and I am convinced that the decisions taken in this case were not only the right ones but the only ones that could responsibly be taken in the circumstances. Having regard to all the circumstances of the case, I do not believe that an inquiry into this matter is justified or warranted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should now like to answer some of the questions raised by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. That right hon. gentleman spoke first of surveillance and the fact that we were maintaining surveillance of a man who had not been brought before the courts. He suggested that this was an injustice. Of course, there is some truth and some basis for an argument of that kind. However, I wonder what the hon. gentleman would have said had I not maintained surveillance of Mr. Spencer, knowing that he in fact had acted in a way which was not in the interests of our national security? I can imagine the type of speech the right hon. gentleman would have made under these circumstances.

I am sure the right hon. gentleman could, having a legal background in criminal law-he knows more about this than I do-in his mind conceive of surveillance which could at the same time protect an individual and prevent him from committing a crime. I am an amateur in law but there is no way in the world that I know of how the R.C.M.P. could at one time prevent a man who has been engaged in espionage activities from engaging further in them and at the same time protect him. As hon. members of the committee are aware, a statement was made by Mr. Spencer to the effect that he and the reporter could in fact be killed for what they were discussing.
When did he say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is the information in a report and I will be glad to inform the right hon. gentleman.
Let us get the facts rather than generalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some time ago-
This is just a sober second thought.
You used the expression yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the right hon. gentleman could use some sober second thoughts.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman also referred to an article written by Mr. Peter Newman. I hope I am not being unfair to Mr. Newman but if I understood the right hon. gentleman correctly-
I never referred to him.
It was Trueman.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry; it was an article by Mr. Trueman to the effect that Mr. Spencer had said that heads would roll in Ottawa and in high places. The right hon. gentleman then asked whether or not we had initiated an investigation by the R.C.M.P. into this situation. We did so and the outcome of that investigation was that Mr. Spencer stated: "Those newspapermen again".
What date was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member could not give any credence to this type of story. Certainly he was not being misquoted in the newspapers.

You certainly were not misquoted on television.
(Mr. Cardin.]
The minister was not misquoted when he used Spencer's name on television.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I used Spencer's name on television after he had identified himself. The right hon. gentleman asked several other questions. I have been considering whether or not I should answer him. He wanted to know something about the amounts of money that were involved. It is unusual to reveal this type of information but in order to prove to the right hon. gentleman that we are not trying to hide anything I intend to go perhaps farther in giving this information than anyone has gone before with the hope that the members of this committee will realize that we are not hiding anything. The amounts of money involved ranged between $3,000 and $4,000. It is difficult to find out the exact amounts because they were paid in the form of travelling and other expenses. As far as we were able to determine, those were the amounts involved in this case.
The right hon. gentleman also asked for the dates on which these alleged offences were supposed to have occurred and he suggested to the committee that by divulging this information we would not be doing any harm to our security.
Just give us the months. That will be sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the years also have some bearing.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The alleged offences started to occur well before 1960. The more serious offences are alleged to have been committed in 1961 and 1962. There were no contacts made between 1963 and the time he was apprehended. As the right hon. gentleman knows, having experience in matters of this kind, the purpose of security and intelligence procedures is not necessarily to establish a charge or to prosecute one but rather to find out as much as possible from the individual in question. That was exactly the situation in this case.
Were the two Russians in question in Canada in 1960?
Yes, or their predecessors.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Do not look so shocked. Do not put on an act. You are not impressing anybody.
They were not here.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
You have been caught putting on an act.

Your second act was interesting.

Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then the right hon. gentleman made reference to a press release that was issued in May and stated that I had denied that something in the statement was correct. The right hon. gentleman knows that there were two people involved and one of them had co-operated with the police. He was referring, I think, to the activities of female employees in the civil service. I said no at the time for the simple reason that this had nothing at all to do with Spencer. I wonder whether the right hon. gentleman understood this. Anyway, I gave him the explanation. He asked for it and that is that. The other question-

speechtext: We want to hear his alibis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is only one other question that I should like to try to clarify if I may. That is the question, which has been repeated on many occasions, that the Prime Minister or somebody stated that we were not prosecuting Spencer because he was ill. It is true that Spencer was ill in May; he was very seriously ill at that time. The statement-any hon. member can look at the record of the statement that was made-was that he was ill and we were looking into whether there were reasons for prosecution. Someone might have interpreted that as meaning that we were not prosecuting Spencer because he was ill but that was never said, nor was it the intention.
The other matter that arises in this connection is the fact that it was very difficult indeed, when the man was actually very ill and in hospital, for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to carry on the inquiries and investigations that were needed at that time. I have given answers to the questions of the right hon. gentleman as best I can and I can assure him and the members of the committee that we have nothing to hide.

Did the former government proceed to prosecute in all security risk cases during their term of office?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman might direct that question to the right hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman.
Can the Minister of Justice give us the answer? The Leader of the Opposition does not want to give us the answer. Could we have the answer to this question from the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it would be in the public interest to do so, Mr. Chairman.
Do we assume that they did not ?

Mr. Chairman, when the
history of the 60's is written the Spencer case, which will probably only appear as a footnote on one page, will not be a reference with regard to which historians of the future will give much credit to this government. We heard a great deal from the Minister of Justice today and the Prime Minister the other day about how for some peculiar reason it is only members of the opposition who are finding fault or asking questions about the Spencer case and the way in which the government has handled it.
I have not had an opportunity to see all the newspapers but I have had an opportunity to see some of the newspaper editorials written since the Prime Minister made his statement last week. I want to put on the record, because the Minister of Justice has perhaps been too busy preparing his case for the reason that it is a weak case, what these newspapers are saying. I shall quote only from Liberal newspapers to show the minister and the Prime Minister that the members of the opposition in this house are not alone in their questions and doubts about this case. Here is the Winnipeg Free Press of Friday, February 25:
The Prime Minister's statement of Wednesday on the Spencer case, although an improvement on its predecessors, does not meet the central criticisms which have been levelled in parliament and in the newspapers against the government's handling of this serious matter-

February 28, 1$66
Supply-Justice
There is no escaping the conclusion that the government, probably with the best of intentions, has acted as a court in the present case.
The Toronto Star of February 25 said:
In his statement in the House of Commons this week on the now notorious Spencer case, Prime Minister Lester Pearson declared: "I do not believe (Mr. Spencer's) rights as a person or as a citizen have been violated. On the contrary, I believe he has been treated with scrupulous fairness."
Few Canadians who have followed this case will agree with the Prime Minister-
The cabinet should do one of two things. Either it should lay charges against Victor Spencer (if necessary the case could be tried in camera to prevent disclosure of state secrets) or it should restore him his job and his pensions rights and take the Mounties off his doorstep.
The Montreal Star said on February 25:
So far as Mr. Pearson is concerned the Spencer case is closed. The Prime Minister may be happy about it all, quite convinced that the interests of national security are not jeapardized, and that no injustice has been worked. No one else is so easily convinced and the suspicion will not down that in this, as in perhaps other cases, the government has something to hide.
The minister today made a great deal of the fact that Mr. Spencer himself disclosed that he was involved. I want to tell the minister that Mr. Spencer did not have to identify himself. The press release issued by the Department of External Affairs was so specific that the postal workers in Vancouver knew that Mr. Spencer must be the person concerned. The press release mentioned that the person involved was sick and in hospital and these workers knew that Mr. Spencer was the person.
Apparently the government is satisfied with its handling of this case. The Prime Minister, of course, is very easily satisfied. It is a characteristic of the Prime Minister that he is easily satisfied. I should like to quote from the Prime Minister's speech of February 23:
-I believe Mr. Spencer's dismissal and his loss of pension rights under the law was lawful and just. I do not believe his rights as a person or as a citizen have been violated. On the contrary, I believe he has been treated with scrupulous fairness.
How was Mr. Spencer treated? In what way was Mr. Spencer heard? I quote again from the speech the Prime Minister made on February 23:
-he was given a hearing by a senior official of the Civil Service Commission, at which he had every opportunity to state his case. Neither at this hearing with a member of the Civil Service Commission present-and the Civil Service Commission has an interest in the protection of the rights of civil servants;-

Etc., etc.
-did Mr. Spencer make any complaint over his dismissal or prospective dismissal, or any complaint about the treatment he had received.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
This is the report which the Prime Minister received from one person in the Civil Service Commission. In outlining procedures for the investigation of government employees accused of having violated security in 1963, the Prime Minister assured the house that procedures would be adopted whereby these employees would be permitted to have a hearing before an independent commission composed of people outside the government service. Mr. Spencer did not have this opportunity. Mr. Spencer had a hearing, if it could be called a hearing, by one member of the Civil Service Commission or one member of its staff.
Is that sufficient for a decision affecting the future life of a government employee? Does not the Minister of Justice, does not the Prime Minister-I see the Postmaster General is in his seat and it is a good thing he is. I should like to remind the Postmaster General-
I am always here.

[DOT]-of a case where an employee of the Post Office Department was dismissed. He exercised his right of appeal, an appeal board was set up and the appeal board rendered a unanimous decision that the employee involved should not be dismissed. However, the Civil Service Commission exercised its judgment and decided that the person should be dismissed. He was dismissed. In that case, Mr. Chairman, it did not suit the government to take the advice of the appeal board. Its advice was ignored. In that case the Civil Service Commission gave the government the kind of advice it wanted so the government followed that advice.
I express no opinion about the guilt of Mr. Spencer. I do not have the evidence. It may be that Mr. Spencer is guilty, although I must express some doubt about the value of secret information which a postal employee could secure and whether or not it would be of real danger to the welfare of the people of Canada.
But I suggest, Mr. Chairman, regardless of what he did, there could be no reason for denying the suggestions which have come from members in every party, including the other side of the house, that a judicial inquiry be held in camera. I cannot believe for a moment, whatever Mr. Spencer is guilty of, that he was able to collect information of
February 28, 1966

greater danger to the people of Canada than did the spies involved in the case which arose out of the disclosures by Igor Gouzenko. In that case the government convened a private judicial hearing. Witnesses were questioned before two judges who were aided by counsel acting for the commission. The judges made a report on the basis of which certain people were prosecuted. In that case information of tremendous importance was transmitted to countries outside of Canada. The government did not hesitate, even under those difficult circumstances, to have a judicial inquiry. There can be no reason, for now saying that we cannot have a hearing before a judge or several judges in camera. These judges may prosecute but certainly there would be no doubt about the guilt or otherwise of Mr. Spencer.
It is not my intention today to say anything further about how Mr. Spencer's rights as an individual were violated. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister is in his seat. In the years before he came to this house, when he was the publisher of a magazine called "Cite Libre", he had the courage to fight the repressive policies of the former premier of Quebec. I wonder what the Parliamentary Secretary, the hon. member for Mount Royal, would have said about this case if he were not here and were not sitting on the government benches? There is no question about how he handled things before he came here, how he felt about civil liberties.

Yes.
